title: Ask the Audience to Experience Your Message Directly
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This Admired Leadership piece argues that speakers make a point most powerfully when they let the audience experience it rather than hear it described. It opens with Khrushchev's secret speech on Stalin, where a heckler's question was answered by silence that proved the speaker's point. The piece generalizes from that story: questions that demand an answer, short audience activities and props all let a speaker demonstrate an emotion or insight instead of describing it. It gives examples such as asking people to stand and point to True North or to examine how they make a fist. The caveat is that the activity must connect to the point and must not feel hokey or frivolous. The closing line ties this to the author's recurring theme that showing rather than telling produces the deepest learning.
points: Khrushchev's "Who said that?" moment shows a speaker can make a listener feel a point instead of hearing about it.
Questions, brief activities and props are the three tools for turning an audience from passive consumers into participants.
The demonstration must connect powerfully to the message and avoid feeling hokey or frivolous.
Direct experience builds a connection between speaker and message that is hard to replicate any other way.
quotes: During the speech, a heckler in the crowd shouted out, “You were there. Why didn’t you stop him?” Khrushchev stopped, looked out into the audience, and said boldly, “Who said that?

He asked again, demanding to know the source. “Who said that?” No hand went up. No one moved or said a word. Khrushchev looked at many faces in the audience and quietly said, “Now you know why we didn’t do anything.

Instead of telling the audience about the emotions he felt, Khrushchev did something great presenters do when they can. He asked the audience to share the emotion or experience with him. When a speaker or presenter asks the audience to directly experience a critical point, they capture attention in a massively powerful way.

When audiences are asked to complete a task with a prop, such as a piece of rope or rubber band, they become immersed in the message rather than passively consume it. Of course, the request and activity must connect powerfully to the point being made.

While not all presentations can include a demonstrative device, when possible, speakers should consider what message points would be best made through direct experience. If the demonstration is not hokey or frivolous, the audience will become much more engaged with the presentation and potentially internalize the message.
